faq.a: In recurrent AOM (≥3 episodes in 6 months) or persistent effusion >3 months with hearing loss, when surgical facilities exist.
faq.q: When is a grommet (ventilation tube) indicated?

faq.a: High local resistance rates; they are reserved for penicillin allergy.
faq.q: Why avoid macrolides as first‑line for AOM?

faq.a: Only if discharge is dry, no systemic signs and ear is clean; otherwise oral antibiotics are required.
faq.q: Can a child with CSOM be safely sent home without antibiotics?

exam: A 2‑year‑old presents with ear pain, fever 38.5 °C and a bulging drum – what is your immediate management? — Start oral amoxicillin, give analgesia, arrange review in 48 h.
A child with chronic ear discharge for 3 weeks has a perforated drum – which investigation is essential and why? — Culture of discharge to guide antibiotic choice; if unavailable, treat empirically.
How does HIV infection alter the presentation of otitis media? — Higher risk of recurrent infections, atypical pathogens, and poorer response to standard antibiotics.
What clinical sign distinguishes otitis externa from otitis media? — Pain on tragus manipulation and external canal erythema point to otitis externa.
A patient with AOM does not improve after 48 h of amoxicillin – what next step? — Assess adherence, consider switch to high‑dose amoxicillin or add clavulanic acid; evaluate for mastoiditis.
Why is pneumococcal vaccination important for middle‑ear disease? — Reduces incidence of S. pneumoniae AOM, the most common bacterial cause.
What are the red‑flag features that mandate referral to a tertiary centre? — Mastoiditis, intracranial signs, persistent high fever, severe hearing loss.
Explain why topical quinolones are preferred for CSOM when available. — They achieve high local concentrations, bypass systemic side‑effects, and have low resistance rates.
ai.title: Paediatric Middle Ear Infections
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: Middle ear disease in children ranges from acute otitis media to chronic suppurative otitis media. Understanding anatomy, risk factors, presentation and limited investigations guides safe management in low‑resource settings.

b: AOM: bulging tympanic membrane, erythema, otalgia < 48 h.
CSOM: perforated drum, otorrhoea, hearing loss.
sections.p: Otitis media refers to inflammation of the middle ear cavity, often with effusion. Acute otitis media (AOM) is a rapid‑onset infection with pain, while chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) is persistent discharge >2 weeks with tympanic membrane perforation.

b: Mild AOM: mild pain, no fever, normal hearing.
Severe AOM: severe pain, fever ≥38 °C, bulging drum.
CSOM stage I: small central perforation, no mastoid disease.
CSOM stage II: large perforation or mastoid involvement.
sections.p: AOM severity is graded by the WHO otitis media severity scale (mild, moderate, severe) based on pain, fever and tympanic membrane findings. CSOM is staged by extent of perforation and presence of mastoiditis.

b: Bacterial: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
Viral prodrome: RSV, rhinovirus, influenza.
Risk factors: daycare, smoke exposure, low birth weight, HIV.
sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings the most common pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae (non‑typeable) and Moraxella catarrhalis. HIV, malnutrition and indoor air pollution increase risk.

b: Ear pain worsened by chewing or lying flat.
Fever >38 °C in acute phase.
Unilateral otorrhoea >2 weeks in chronic disease.
sections.p: Children with AOM often refuse to lie down, pull at the ear, have fever and reduced appetite. CSOM presents with persistent foul‑smelling otorrhoea, hearing loss and possible mastoid tenderness.

t.b: Confirms presence of effusion, bulging or perforation; guides diagnosis.
Distinguishes fluid‑filled middle ear (type B) from normal compliance (type A).
Identifies bacterial pathogen and antibiotic susceptibility.

b: Persistent fever >48 h despite antibiotics.
Post‑auricular swelling or tenderness → mastoiditis.
Neurological signs (headache, vomiting, seizures) → intracranial spread.
Sudden severe hearing loss → cholesteatoma.
sections.p: Complications are rare but life‑threatening; early recognition is essential.

b: CSOM: Clean ear gently, apply topical quinolone (e.g., ciprofloxacin) if available; oral amoxicillin if systemic signs.
Ear wick or grommet placement only in referral centre.
sections.p: Treat the infection, relieve pain and prevent complications. In low‑resource settings prioritize oral antibiotics and simple analgesia.

b: Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) reduces S. pneumoniae AOM.
Hib vaccine lowers H. influenzae middle‑ear disease.
Educate caregivers on avoiding smoke exposure and proper feeding position.
sections.p: Re‑examine after 48‑72 h for AOM; after 2 weeks for CSOM. Vaccination and hygiene reduce incidence.

b: Otitis externa – pain worsens with tragus manipulation, external canal erythema.
Mastoiditis – post‑auricular swelling, erythema, systemic toxicity.
Foreign body in ear – visible object, no tympanic membrane bulge.
sections.p: Differential diagnoses share ear pain or discharge but have distinct features.

b: Normal otoscopy early in viral AOM – fluid may be hidden; rely on symptoms.
Negative culture in CSOM after prior antibiotics – still treat empirically.
sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite serious disease.
